claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study describing statistical methods for accounting for population structure.

claims.claim: The HMDP is sufficiently powered to detect loci with small effect sizes for a given trait.
claims.source: Importantly, the HMDP is sufficiently powered to detect loci with small effect sizes for a given trait (Bennett et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the original HMDP study demonstrating its statistical power.

claims.claim: The HMDP was first studied in 2010 to perform fine mapping of plasma lipids.
claims.source: The HMDP was first studied in 2010, to perform fine mapping of plasma lipids (Bennett et al., 2010) and has since been used to identify novel loci for blood (Davis et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2015), bone (Calabrese et al., 2012; Farber et al., 2011; Hiyari et al., 2015), inflammatory (Pirie et al., 2019; Orozco et al., 2012; Hiyari et al., 2015; Buscher et al., 2017), auditory (Boussaty et al., 2020; Lavinsky et al., 2015; Lavinsky et al., 2016) and behavioural traits (Park et al., 2011) in addition to cardiometabolic diseases and related traits, which we will focus on in this review (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies using the HMDP for various trait mapping.

claims.claim: Parker and colleagues integrated genetic data with liver proteomics and lipidomics, as well as plasma lipidomics from 107 HMDP strains to explore the genetic regulation of the hepatic and plasma lipidome.
claims.source: For example, to explore the genetic regulation of the hepatic and plasma lipidome, Parker and colleagues integrated genetic data with liver proteomics and lipidomics, as well as plasma lipidomics from 107 HMDP strains, in the absence of intervention (Parker et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the Parker et al. study that performed this integrative analysis.

claims.claim: The Ath-HMDP consists of >100 genetically diverse F1 hybrid atherosclerosis-prone mice generated by interbreeding male C57BL/6J mice with humanised lipid profiles with female HMDP mice.
claims.source: In this body of work, male C57BL/6J mice with humanised lipid profiles, via transgenic expression of the human cholesteryl ester transferase protein (CETP) transgene (Jiang et al., 1992) and the human apolipoprotein (APO)E*3-Leiden variant (van den Maagdenberg et al., 1993), were interbred with female HMDP mice to generate a panel of >100 genetically diverse F1 hybrid atherosclerosis-prone mice.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies describing the transgenic models and the Ath-HMDP breeding scheme.

claims.claim: Ath-HMDP hybrid offspring were fed a high-fat, high-cholesterol (western) diet for 16 weeks.
claims.source: Hybrid offspring were subsequently fed a high-fat, high-cholesterol (western) diet for 16 weeks (Ath-HMDP; Figure 1; Bennett et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the Bennett et al. study describing the Ath-HMDP experimental design.

claims.claim: Ath-HMDP studies identified many novel genes mapping to plaque burden and atherosclerosis-related traits.
claims.source: These studies identified many novel genes mapping to plaque burden and atherosclerosis-related traits, and have been used as a complementary resource to omics data generated from human tissues to identify evolutionarily conserved pathways that drive atherosclerosis, and prioritise high confidence candidates for further investigation (Talukdar et al., 2016; Koplev et al., 2022; von Scheidt et al., 2017; Cohain et al., 2021; Kessler et al., 2017; Bauer et al., 2022; von Scheidt et al., 2021; Li et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies using the Ath-HMDP for gene discovery.

claims.claim: Rau and colleagues treated mice from 105 strains of the HMDP with isoproterenol for 21 days to mimic features of heart failure (HF-HMDP).
claims.source: To explore the genetic architecture of HF, Rau and colleagues treated mice from 105 strains of the HMDP with isoproterenol for 21 days to mimic features of heart failure (HF-HMDP; Figure 1; Rau et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the Rau et al. study describing the HF-HMDP experimental design.

claims.claim: The HF-HMDP platform has provided insights into the genetic regulation of traits related to cardiac dysfunction including cardiac remodelling, hypertrophy, diastolic dysfunction, and altered cardiomyocyte metabolism.
claims.source: Further studies have leveraged this platform to provide insights into the genetic regulation of traits related to cardiac dysfunction including cardiac remodelling (Wang et al., 2016), hypertrophy (Santolini et al., 2018; Rau et al., 2017; Krishnan et al., 2022), diastolic dysfunction (Wang et al., 2019; Cao et al., 2022) and altered cardiomyocyte metabolism (Seldin et al., 2017), and further facilitated the identification of transmembrane glycoprotein NMB (GPNMB) as a potential plasma biomarker for left ventricular mass (Lin et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies using the HF-HMDP for various cardiac trait analyses.

claims.claim: HMDP mice were subjected to an 8-week HF/HS diet alongside chow-fed control mice to explore the genetic drivers of diet-induced obesity and gut microbiota (HF/HS-HMDP).
claims.source: HMDP mice have also been subjected to lifestyle interventions such as an 8-week HF/HS diet (HF/HS-HMDP; Figure 1), alongside chow-fed control mice, to explore the genetic drivers of diet-induced obesity and gut microbiota (Parks et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the Parks et al. study describing the HF/HS-HMDP experimental design.

claims.claim: The HF/HS-HMDP platform has been used to elucidate genetic mechanisms that regulate hepatic triglyceride content, hepatic lipids, and sex- and tissue-specific mechanisms of NAFLD.
claims.source: Subsequent studies have used this platform to elucidate genetic mechanisms that regulate hepatic triglyceride (TG) content (Hui et al., 2015), hepatic lipids (Norheim et al., 2021Norheim et al., 2018), sex- and tissue-specific mechanisms of NAFLD (Chella Krishnan et al., 2018; Norheim et al., 2021; Parks et al., 2015; Kurt et al., 2018; Norheim et al., 2017; Chella Krishnan et al., 2021a) and phenotypes linked to adiposity, mitochondrial function, and insulin resistance (Civelek et al., 2017; Chella Krishnan et al., 2019; Chella Krishnan et al., 2021b; Schugar et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies using the HF/HS-HMDP for various metabolic trait analyses.

claims.claim: A 15-strain subset of the HMDP was subjected to 30 days of voluntary wheel-running (Ex-HMDP) to identify novel mechanisms that regulate mitochondrial biogenesis and bioenergetics in skeletal muscle.
claims.source: Finally, the HMDP has been utilised to provide novel insights into the genetic and molecular mechanisms underpinning protective metabolic interventions. For example, a 15-strain subset of the HMDP was subjected to 30 days of voluntary wheel-running (Ex-HMDP; Figure 1) to identify novel mechanisms that regulate mitochondrial biogenesis and bioenergetics in skeletal muscle (Moore et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the Moore et al. study describing the Ex-HMDP experimental design.

claims.claim: The genes and gene regulatory networks that modulate biological processes in mice are largely conserved in humans.
claims.source: Importantly, emerging studies have demonstrated that the genes and gene regulatory networks that modulate biological processes in mice are largely conserved in humans (Li et al., 2020; Talukdar et al., 2016; Koplev et al., 2022; von Scheidt et al., 2017; Benegiamo et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating cross-species conservation of gene networks.

claims.claim: Cross-species concordance demonstrates that many of the genetic mechanisms that underlie human disease can be accurately identified using mouse GRPs.
claims.source: This cross-species concordance demonstrates that many of the genetic mechanisms that underlie human disease can indeed be accurately identified using mouse GRPs, confirming that integration of mouse and human data is advantageous in this context.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation of cross-species conservation of genetic mechanisms.

claims.claim: Research has shifted focus in the post-GWAS era from discovery of novel genetic variants to downstream elucidation of biological function.
claims.source: With thousands of genetic loci having been identified in human GWAS, research has shifted focus in the post-GWAS era from discovery of novel genetic variants to downstream elucidation of biological function.
claims.evidence: This reflects the current state of the field as described in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The discovery rate of susceptible loci exceeds the capacity to perform time-consuming validation experiments.
claims.source: However, the discovery rate of susceptible loci exceeds the capacity to perform the time-consuming validation experiments (Stacey et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study discussing the challenge of validating GWAS findings.

claims.claim: Integrating complementary human and mouse resources can help pinpoint potential causal genes and offer novel insight into how they cause disease.
claims.source: Integrating complementary human and mouse resources can further help to pinpoint the potential causal genes and offer novel insight into how they cause disease, allowing the most promising targets to be prioritised for downstream analysis (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the advantages of cross-species integration described throughout the manuscript.

claims.claim: Mice have 19 pairs of autosomal chromosomes, compared with 22 in humans.
claims.source: With regard to genetic architecture, mice have 19 pairs of autosomal chromosomes, compared with 22 in humans.
claims.evidence: This is a factual statement about the chromosomal differences between mice and humans.

claims.claim: Many features remain consistent between human and mouse genomes, albeit they have been rearranged in large, conserved regions known as synteny blocks.
claims.source: Despite these obvious structural differences, it is clear that many features remain consistent between genomes, albeit they have been rearranged in large, conserved regions, known as synteny blocks, reflecting divergence of human and mouse lineages ~75 million years ago (Nadeau and Taylor, 1984; Waterston et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies describing synteny between human and mouse genomes.

claims.claim: Human and mouse genomes each contain ~30,000 protein-coding genes.
claims.source: Human and mouse genomes each contain ~30,000 protein-coding genes (Waterston et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study quantifying protein-coding genes in human and mouse genomes.

claims.claim: Approximately 80% of mouse genes can be mapped to a single orthologous gene within the human genome.
claims.source: Approximately 80% of mouse genes can be mapped to a single orthologous gene (i.e. 1:1 orthologues) within the human genome and >99% map to one or more orthologous genes (Waterston et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study quantifying orthology between human and mouse genomes.

claims.claim: Approximately 19% of mouse genes contain more than one orthologue due to lineage-specific duplication events.
claims.source: Hence, ~19% of mouse genes contain more than one orthologue due to lineage-specific duplication events.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the statement that >99% of mouse genes map to one or more human orthologues while 80% map to a single orthologue.

claims.claim: Three ApoE isoforms (ApoE2, ApoE3, and ApoE4) exist in humans, while only a single ApoE isoform exists in mice.
claims.source: Such is the case for ApoE, of which three isoforms (ApoE2, ApoE3, and ApoE4) exist in humans, while only a single ApoE isoform exists in mice (Getz and Reardon, 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study describing ApoE isoforms in humans and mice.

claims.claim: Human ApoE isoforms are structurally and functionally distinct and have different effects on lipoprotein metabolism and disease.
claims.source: The resulting isoforms are structurally and functionally distinct and thus have different effects on lipoprotein metabolism, and indeed disease (Davignon et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study describing the functional differences between ApoE isoforms.

claims.claim: The relative contribution of a gene, gene network, or molecular pathway to a disease will often vary with respect to disease severity.
claims.source: Furthermore, the relative contribution of a gene, gene network, or molecular pathway to a disease will often vary with respect to disease severity.
claims.evidence: This reflects established understanding about the complexity of disease mechanisms.

claims.claim: It is often difficult to accurately quantify the progression of complex diseases, where multiple insults and molecular pathways can contribute to disease pathology.
claims.source: Thus, an important consideration is the use of appropriate preclinical disease models that exhibit clinically relevant features with appropriate severity. A major challenge here is that it is often difficult to accurately quantify the progression of complex diseases, where multiple insults and indeed molecular pathways can contribute to disease pathology.
claims.evidence: This reflects established understanding about the challenges in modeling complex diseases.

claims.claim: The current paradigm suggests that multiple 'hits' are required for NAFLD/NASH progression in genetically predisposed individuals.
claims.source: Such is the case for NAFLD/NASH, where the current paradigm suggests that multiple 'hits' (i.e. insulin resistance, hepatic lipid accumulation, inflammation, etc.) are required for disease progression in genetically predisposed individuals (Buzzetti et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study describing the multiple-hit hypothesis for NAFLD/NASH.

claims.claim: Bona fide, reliable biomarkers for NAFLD/NASH are still mostly lacking, leading to inconsistent phenotyping.
claims.source: While liver biopsy or MRI provide a surrogate measure of NAFLD/NASH, bona fide, reliable biomarkers are still mostly lacking, leading to inconsistent phenotyping between individuals and indeed across different experimental settings, hampering cross-species integration.
claims.evidence: This reflects current knowledge about the challenges in NAFLD/NASH diagnosis and phenotyping.

claims.claim: Selecting therapeutic targets in humans that have evidence of genetic linkage with the disease under investigation more than doubles the success rate of drugs that enter the clinical pipeline.
claims.source: This is underscored by recent evidence indicating that selecting therapeutic targets in humans that have evidence of genetic linkage with the disease under investigation more than doubles the success rate of drugs that enter the clinical pipeline (Nelson et al., 2015; King et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating improved drug development success rates for genetically supported targets.

claims.claim: Preclinical studies are often performed in only a single strain of mice, commonly C57BL/6J in the context of metabolic studies.
claims.source: Clinical translation has likely been hampered by the fact that preclinical studies are often performed in only a single strain of mice, commonly C57BL/6J in the context of metabolic studies, which is not reflective of the genetic and phenotypic heterogeneity of a human population.
claims.evidence: This reflects common practice in preclinical research as described in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Most mouse strains exhibit metabolic dysfunction in response to high-fat diet feeding, albeit with varying magnitude.
claims.source: For example, while most strains (including C57BL/6J) exhibit metabolic dysfunction in response to high-fat diet feeding, albeit with varying magnitude, certain strains are protected from diet-induced insulin resistance (i.e. BALB/c, WSB/EiJ and CAST/EiJ), hepatic fibrosis (i.e. CAST/EiJ), or weight gain (i.e. A/J, WSB/EiJ and CAST/EiJ), while others (i.e. PWK/PhJ) are more susceptible (Montgomery et al., 2013; Bachmann et al., 2022; Benegiamo et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating strain-specific responses to high-fat diet.

claims.claim: Certain mouse strains (BALB/c, WSB/EiJ and CAST/EiJ) are protected from diet-induced insulin resistance.
claims.source: For example, while most strains (including C57BL/6J) exhibit metabolic dysfunction in response to high-fat diet feeding, albeit with varying magnitude, certain strains are protected from diet-induced insulin resistance (i.e. BALB/c, WSB/EiJ and CAST/EiJ), hepatic fibrosis (i.e. CAST/EiJ), or weight gain (i.e. A/J, WSB/EiJ and CAST/EiJ), while others (i.e. PWK/PhJ) are more susceptible (Montgomery et al., 2013; Bachmann et al., 2022; Benegiamo et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating strain-specific protection from insulin resistance.

claims.claim: An increase in energy expenditure was observed in response to a protein-restricted diet in male and female C57BL/6J mice, but not in DBA/2J or Het3 mice.
claims.source: Furthermore, an increase in energy expenditure was observed in response to a protein-restricted diet in male and female C57BL/6J mice, but not in DBA/2J or Het3 mice (Green et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study demonstrating strain-specific responses to protein restriction.

claims.claim: Cross-species interrogation can be useful for pinpointing candidate genes that contribute to polygenic diseases.
claims.source: Thus, cross-species interrogation can be useful for pinpointing candidate genes that contribute to polygenic diseases.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the example provided of using cross-species data to identify PVRL2 as a candidate gene for atherosclerosis.

claims.claim: SNP rs2075650 near APOE and APOC1 in humans has been associated with CAD risk.
claims.source: For example, SNPs such as rs2075650 near APOE and APOC1 in humans, genes that have well established roles in lipid metabolism and atherosclerosis, have been associated with CAD risk (Deloukas et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a GWAS study identifying this association.

claims.claim: A significant correlation between aortic root lesion area and the expression of Pvrl2 was identified across the Ath-HMDP in both the aorta and liver.
claims.source: A significant correlation between aortic root lesion area and the expression of poliovirus receptor related 2 (Pvrl2, also known as Nectin-2 or Cd112) was identified across the Ath-HMDP in both the aorta and liver.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on data from the Ath-HMDP study as described in the text.

claims.claim: Pvrl2 is found in the same locus as APOE and APOC1 and was speculated to partly mediate the effect of rs2075650.
claims.source: This gene is found in the same locus as APOE and APOC1 and was speculated to partly mediate the effect of rs2075650 (Bennett et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the co-localization of Pvrl2 with APOE and APOC1, as reported in the cited study.

claims.claim: Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) is a global expression analysis tool that aims to identify modules of co-expressed genes.
claims.source: One such approach is weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA), a global expression analysis tool developed by Zhang and Horvath, 2005, that aims to identify modules of co-expressed genes.
claims.evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by citation to the original WGCNA methodology paper.

claims.claim: Talukdar and colleagues integrated gene expression from seven tissues from individuals with late-stage CAD from the STAGE cohort to construct tissue-specific and cross-tissue co-expression modules for CAD phenotypes.
claims.source: Using this approach, Talukdar and colleagues integrated gene expression from seven tissues obtained from individuals with late-stage CAD from the Stockholm Atherosclerosis Gene Expression (STAGE) cohort, to construct tissue-specific and cross-tissue co-expression modules for CAD phenotypes (Talukdar et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the Talukdar et al. study describing this integrative analysis.

claims.claim: Talukdar and colleagues identified 30 'CAD-causal' modules consisting of genes which contained either a cis-eQTL or had previously been reported in human CAD GWAS.
claims.source: This led to the identification of 30 'CAD-causal' modules consisting of genes which contained either a cis-eQTL or had previously been reported in human CAD GWAS.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on findings from the Talukdar et al. study as described in the text.

claims.claim: 46% of the CAD-causal modules identified by Talukdar and colleagues were associated with phenotypes related to atherosclerosis in Ath-HMDP mice.
claims.source: Integration with phenomic and multi-tissue global gene expression data from 105 strains of mice from the Ath-HMDP revealed that 46% of the CAD-causal modules were associated with phenotypes related to atherosclerosis in mice.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on findings from the Talukdar et al. study as described in the text.

claims.claim: Talukdar and colleagues identified one tissue-specific regulated gene network in aorta, containing 109 genes, that was enriched 2.5-fold in association with lesion size across the Ath-HMDP.
claims.source: Among these, they identified one tissue-specific regulated gene network in aorta, containing 109 genes, that was enriched 2.5-fold in association with lesion size across the Ath-HMDP.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on findings from the Talukdar et al. study as described in the text.

claims.claim: The aortic gene network identified by Talukdar and colleagues was shown to be regulated by seven key driver genes using the key driver analysis algorithm.
claims.source: Using the key driver analysis (KDA) algorithm, this network was shown to be regulated by seven key driver genes, or 'hub genes'.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on findings from the Talukdar et al. study as described in the text.

claims.claim: Independent siRNA knockdown of four key driver genes identified by Talukdar and colleagues activated other genes within the network and modulated THP-1 foam cell formation.
claims.source: Indeed, independent small interfering RNA knockdown of four key driver genes activated other genes within the network and modulated THP-1 foam cell formation, validating their involvement in the regulation of atherosclerosis.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on experimental validation performed in the Talukdar et al. study as described in the text.

claims.claim: SNPs in genes that regulate lipid and glucose pathways can contribute to atherosclerosis susceptibility.
claims.source: SNPs in genes that regulate lipid and glucose pathways can contribute to atherosclerosis susceptibility (Björkegren and Lusis, 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review discussing the role of lipid and glucose pathways in atherosclerosis.

claims.claim: Cohain and colleagues identified a glucose and lipid determining module (GLD) that was negatively associated with cholesterol traits and positively associated with glucose traits.
claims.source: One such module, termed the glucose and lipid determining module (GLD), was negatively associated with cholesterol traits and positively associated with glucose traits.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on findings from the Cohain et al. study as described in the text.

claims.claim: The association between the GLD co-expression module and glucose and lipid traits was replicated in two independent human cohorts and in mice from the HMDP and Ath-HMDP.
claims.source: Furthermore, the association between the GLD co-expression module and glucose and lipid traits was replicated in two independent human cohorts and in mice from the HMDP and the Ath-HMDP.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on findings from the Cohain et al. study as described in the text.

claims.claim: Four key driver genes identified in the GLD module are known regulators of cholesterol biosynthesis.
claims.source: Four key driver genes were identified, all of which are known regulators of cholesterol biosynthesis.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on findings from the Cohain et al. study as described in the text.

claims.claim: The ability to reconstruct the GLD module across several independent human and mouse cohorts provides indication that this module and the four predicted key drivers are evolutionarily conserved mediators of glucose and cholesterol metabolism.
claims.source: Notably, the ability to reconstruct the GLD module across several independent human and mouse cohorts provides a clear indication that this module and the four predicted key drivers are evolutionarily conserved mediators of glucose and cholesterol metabolism.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the replication of the GLD module across multiple cohorts as described in the text.

claims.claim: Chella Krishnan and colleagues demonstrated that adipose mitochondrial OXPHOS genes were elevated in female mice across the HF/HS-HMDP in a tissue-specific and sexually dimorphic manner.
claims.source: In a separate study, Chella Krishnan and colleagues demonstrated that adipose mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) genes were elevated in female mice across the HF/HS-HMDP in a tissue-specific and sexually dimorphic manner.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on findings from the Chella Krishnan et al. study as described in the text.

claims.claim: The elevation of adipose mitochondrial OXPHOS genes in female mice was conserved across the human STARNET and GTEx cohorts.
claims.source: This effect was conserved across the human STARNET and GTEx cohorts (Chella Krishnan et al., 2021b).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on findings from the Chella Krishnan et al. study as described in the text.

claims.claim: An association was observed between mitochondrial DNA levels and metabolic traits such as body weight and insulin resistance across the HF/HS-HMDP that was conserved across the human METSIM cohort.
claims.source: An association was also observed between mitochondrial DNA levels and metabolic traits such as body weight and insulin resistance across the HF/HS-HMDP that was conserved across the human METSIM cohort.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on findings from the Chella Krishnan et al. study as described in the text.

claims.claim: Association mapping of the HF/HS-HMDP led to the identification of a female-specific trans-eQTL regulated by Ndufv2 that controlled the expression of 89 genes, of which approximately one third were OXPHOS genes.
claims.source: Association mapping of the HF/HS-HMDP led to the identification of a female-specific trans-eQTL regulated by NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase core subunit V2 (Ndufv2) that controlled the expression of 89 genes, of which approximately one third were OXPHOS genes.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on findings from the Chella Krishnan et al. study as described in the text.

claims.claim: Validation experiments confirmed a causal role for Ndufv2 in the sex-specific regulation of obesity via alterations in mitochondrial function.
claims.source: Subsequent validation experiments confirmed a causal role for Ndufv2 in the sex-specific regulation of obesity via alterations in mitochondrial function.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on experimental validation performed in the Chella Krishnan et al. study as described in the text.

claims.claim: In ~500 HF/HS-fed DO mice, Keller and colleagues identified genetic variants in pancreatic islets associated with diabetes-related traits in vivo and in cultured islets treated ex vivo with insulin secretagogues.
claims.source: For example, in ~500 HF/HS-fed DO mice, Keller and colleagues identified genetic variants in pancreatic islets associated with diabetes-related traits in vivo, including plasma insulin and glucose levels following fasting, or in response to an oral glucose tolerance test (Keller et al., 2018), and in cultured islets treated ex vivo with insulin secretagogues (Keller et al., 2019), as previously mentioned.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the Keller et al. studies describing these findings.

claims.claim: Syntenic regions containing mouse in vivo and ex vivo QTL identified by Keller and colleagues were significantly enriched with diabetes-related SNPs in humans.
claims.source: The authors observed that syntenic regions containing mouse in vivo and ex vivo QTL were significantly enriched with diabetes-related SNPs in humans, with over half of the ex vivo QTL mapping to one or more diabetes-related traits in humans.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on findings from the Keller et al. studies as described in the text.

claims.claim: Using the HMDP, PSMD9 was identified and experimentally validated as a novel regulator of hepatic and plasma TG and DG abundance.
claims.source: For example, using the HMDP, proteasome 26S subunit, non-ATPase 9 (PSMD9) was identified and experimentally validated as a novel regulator of hepatic and plasma TG and diglyceride (DG) abundance (Parker et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the Parker et al. study that identified and validated PSMD9.

claims.claim: Using S-PrediXcan, hepatic PSMD9 expression was associated with several readouts of adiposity in the UK Biobank.
claims.source: These findings were complemented by analysis using S-PrediXcan (Barbeira et al., 2018), in which hepatic PSMD9 expression was associated with several readouts of adiposity in the UK Biobank.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on findings from the Parker et al. study as described in the text.

claims.claim: A small GWAS linked PSMD9 to obesity and T2D.
claims.source: Further supporting this, a small GWAS linked PSMD9 to obesity and T2D (Gragnoli and Cronsell, 2007; Gragnoli, 2010; Gragnoli, 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to GWAS studies linking PSMD9 to obesity and T2D.

claims.claim: Lin and colleagues demonstrated that Gpnmb was significantly upregulated in the setting of HF in the MAGNet consortium, similar to the effect observed in HF-HMDP mice.
claims.source: They complemented their findings by overlaying human cardiac transcriptomic data, which demonstrated that Gpnmb was significantly upregulated in the setting of HF in the MAGNet consortium, similar to the effect observed in HF-HMDP mice.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on findings from the Lin et al. study as described in the text.

claims.claim: Cardiac GPNMB protein expression was increased in two separate murine models of HF.
claims.source: Furthermore, cardiac GPNMB protein expression was increased in two separate murine models of HF, whilst plasma GPNMB abundance was reciprocally attenuated in the setting of HF in humans and mice, suggesting that plasma GPNMB may possess diagnostic or prognostic utility as a biomarker for HF.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on findings from the Lin et al. study as described in the text.

claims.claim: Plasma GPNMB abundance was reciprocally attenuated in the setting of HF in humans and mice.
claims.source: Furthermore, cardiac GPNMB protein expression was increased in two separate murine models of HF, whilst plasma GPNMB abundance was reciprocally attenuated in the setting of HF in humans and mice, suggesting that plasma GPNMB may possess diagnostic or prognostic utility as a biomarker for HF.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on findings from the Lin et al. study as described in the text.

claims.claim: Plasma GPNMB may possess diagnostic or prognostic utility as a biomarker for HF.
claims.source: Furthermore, cardiac GPNMB protein expression was increased in two separate murine models of HF, whilst plasma GPNMB abundance was reciprocally attenuated in the setting of HF in humans and mice, suggesting that plasma GPNMB may possess diagnostic or prognostic utility as a biomarker for HF.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the observed changes in plasma GPNMB in HF.

claims.claim: Li and colleagues performed WGCNA using liver expression data from the HMDP and DO mouse populations to construct mouse liver co-expression modules.
claims.source: Indeed, in a recent study, Li and colleagues performed WGCNA using liver expression data obtained from the HMDP and DO mouse populations to construct mouse liver co-expression modules (Li et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the Li et al. study describing this analysis.

claims.claim: Li and colleagues identified a cholesterol module of 2435 genes, of which 112 consistently replicated across datasets.
claims.source: The enrichment of genes for the 'cholesterol biosynthetic process' Gene Ontology term identified a cholesterol module of 2435 genes, of which 112 consistently replicated across datasets.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on findings from the Li et al. study as described in the text.

claims.claim: Integration of 112 cholesterol module genes with human GWAS SNPs for plasma lipids prioritised a subset of 48 autosomal genes, 25 of which were novel.
claims.source: They next integrated the 112 genes with SNPs for plasma total cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein (LDL)-cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein (HDL)-cholesterol, and TG levels from the Global Lipid Genetics Consortium human GWAS, which prioritised a subset of 48 autosomal genes, 25 of which were novel, that were below the genome-wide and sub-threshold significance.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on findings from the Li et al. study as described in the text.

claims.claim: Of the 25 prioritised genes identified by Li and colleagues, many corresponding loci were replicated in association with plasma lipid traits across the MVP and UK Biobank human lipid GWAS datasets.
claims.source: Of the 25 prioritised genes, many corresponding loci were replicated in association with plasma lipid traits across the Million Veteran Program (MVP) and UK Biobank human lipid GWAS datasets.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on findings from the Li et al. study as described in the text.

claims.claim: von Scheidt and colleagues catalogued 827 genes from experimental mouse models that significantly altered lesion size or plaque stability.
claims.source: With regard to non-directed integration of data obtained from human and mouse populations, von Scheidt and colleagues comprehensively explored the literature and catalogued all the genes from experimental mouse models that significantly altered lesion size or plaque stability (827 genes from over 9000 publications) and compared them with orthologous human GWAS-derived genes for CAD (244 genes from 169 significant and suggestive GWAS loci).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the von Scheidt et al. study that performed this comprehensive literature review.

claims.claim: von Scheidt and colleagues identified 244 orthologous human GWAS-derived genes for CAD from 169 significant and suggestive GWAS loci.
claims.source: With regard to non-directed integration of data obtained from human and mouse populations, von Scheidt and colleagues comprehensively explored the literature and catalogued all the genes from experimental mouse models that significantly altered lesion size or plaque stability (827 genes from over 9000 publications) and compared them with orthologous human GWAS-derived genes for CAD (244 genes from 169 significant and suggestive GWAS loci).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the von Scheidt et al. study that identified these genes.

claims.claim: Only 46 orthologous GWAS-derived genes had been studied in mice, 45 of which significantly impacted atherosclerosis.
claims.source: They demonstrated that only 46 orthologous GWAS-derived genes had been studied in mice, 45 of which significantly impacted atherosclerosis (von Scheidt et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on findings from the von Scheidt et al. study as described in the text.

claims.claim: Over 50% of the enriched CAD pathways were concordant between mice and humans.
claims.source: Furthermore, pathway enrichment analysis for gene sets in the human GWAS and the gene set of 827 mouse atherosclerosis genes revealed that over 50% of the enriched CAD pathways were concordant between mice and humans.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on findings from the von Scheidt et al. study as described in the text.

claims.claim: Of the 244 human GWAS-derived CAD genes, the expression of 66 (27%) orthologous genes in the aorta and 27 (11%) genes in the liver correlated with lesion size in the Ath-HMDP.
claims.source: The authors also examined the variation in lesion size across the Ath-HMDP and found that, of the 244 human GWAS-derived CAD genes, the expression of 66 (27%) orthologous genes in the aorta and 27 (11%) genes in the liver correlated with lesion size.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on findings from the von Scheidt et al. study as described in the text.

claims.claim: The expression of 151 of 274 (55%) mouse orthologous genes in liver and adipose tissue correlated with plasma lipids across the Ath-HMDP.
claims.source: By overlaying two human lipid GWAS (274 genes) with plasma lipids from the Ath-HMDP they demonstrated that the expression of 151 of 274 (55%) mouse orthologous genes in liver and adipose tissue correlated with plasma lipids across strains.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on findings from the von Scheidt et al. study as described in the text.

claims.claim: There is substantial conservation of genetic mechanisms and biological pathways that influence atherosclerosis in mice and humans.
claims.source: This study demonstrates that there is substantial conservation of genetic mechanisms and biological pathways that influence atherosclerosis in mice and humans and provides a rich resource of cross-species conserved genes for further analysis.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the findings of the von Scheidt et al. study showing concordance between mouse and human atherosclerosis genes and pathways.

claims.claim: Bioinformatic analysis predicted MAFF/Maff and ATF3/Atf3 to orchestrate a liver network enriched in genes linked to atherosclerosis.
claims.source: Through investigating gene regulatory networks in atherosclerosis, these studies predicted MAFF/Maff and ATF3/Atf3 to orchestrate a liver network enriched in genes linked to atherosclerosis.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on findings from follow-up studies (Bauer et al., 2022; von Scheidt et al., 2021) as described in the text.

claims.claim: MAFF/Maff and ATF3/Atf3 regulate lipid metabolism and atherosclerosis in an inflammation-dependent manner.
claims.source: These findings were validated in silico and in vitro, suggesting that MAFF/Maff and ATF3/Atf3 regulate lipid metabolism and atherosclerosis in an inflammation-dependent manner.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on validation experiments performed in the follow-up studies as described in the text.

claims.claim: Hui and colleagues combined GWAS analysis with liver transcriptomic data from 102 strains of the Ath-HMDP to identify genetic loci that contribute to hepatic fibrosis.
claims.source: Hui and colleagues combined GWAS analysis with liver transcriptomic data from 102 strains of the Ath-HMDP to identify genetic loci that contribute to hepatic fibrosis, a key feature of NASH (Hui et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the Hui et al. study describing this analysis.

claims.claim: Hui and colleagues identified several cis-eQTLs, including those for Phactr2 and Eif3h, the gene expression of which significantly correlated with liver fibrosis.
claims.source: This led to the identification of several cis-eQTLs, including those for phosphatase and actin regulator 2 (Phactr2) and eukaryotic translation initiation factor 3 subunit H (Eif3h), the gene expression of which significantly correlated with liver fibrosis.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on findings from the Hui et al. study as described in the text.

claims.claim: A 60% overlap between mouse and human NASH sub-networks was identified by Hui and colleagues.
claims.source: Using marker set enrichment analysis to identify GWAS signals that were overrepresented among eQTLs mapped to individual pathways, a 60% overlap between mouse and human NASH sub-networks was identified.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on findings from the Hui et al. study as described in the text.

claims.claim: Hui and colleagues identified nine pathways that were shared between mouse and human NASH.
claims.source: Specifically, they identified nine pathways that were shared between mouse and human (e.g. innate and adaptive immune system), in addition to six mouse-specific (e.g. fatty acid, TG, and ketone body metabolism) and twelve human-specific (e.g. cytokine signalling) pathways.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on findings from the Hui et al. study as described in the text.

claims.claim: Statistical causal inference techniques such as cis-expression correlation or mediation analysis are useful in prioritising genes that are likely to be causally associated with a given SNP.
claims.source: Indeed, statistical causal inference techniques such as cis-expression correlation or mediation analysis are useful in prioritising the gene(s) that are likely to be causally associated with a given SNP.
claims.evidence: This reflects established knowledge about statistical methods used in systems genetics.

claims.claim: If phenotypic components are tightly correlated, this can inflate mediation statistics and increase the rate of false positives.
claims.source: However, if phenotypic components themselves are tightly correlated, as is often the case for functionally related genes, proteins, and lipid species, this can inflate mediation statistics and increase the rate of false positives.
claims.evidence: This reflects established understanding about limitations of mediation analysis.

claims.claim: Network modelling approaches such as WGCNA or Bayesian networking are prone to false positive relationships due to inherent limitations in modeling complex biological systems.
claims.source: Despite advances in statistical network modelling approaches such as WGCNA or Bayesian networking and its derivative KDA algorithm, these approaches are prone to false positive relationships due to inherent limitations in the modelling of complex and dynamic biological systems, or simply the result of bystander genes.
claims.evidence: This reflects established understanding about limitations of network modeling approaches.

claims.claim: Validation experiments are required to establish causality and confirm directionality of associations identified through systems genetics approaches.
claims.source: However, this does not obviate the requirement for validation experiments to establish causality and confirm directionality.
claims.evidence: This reflects established understanding about the necessity of experimental validation in systems genetics.

claims.claim: Adenoviral overexpression of PSMD9 for 5–7 days promoted the accrual of DG and TG species in C57BL/6J and DBA/2J mice fed a chow diet.
claims.source: In two distinct strains of mice, C57BL/6J and DBA/2J, adenoviral overexpression of PSMD9 for 5–7 days promoted the accrual of DG and TG species in mice fed a chow diet.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on experimental validation performed in the Parker et al. study as described in the text.

claims.claim: In mice fed a western diet for 28 days, PSMD9-antisense oligonucleotide treatment was associated with a significant attenuation of hepatic and plasma TG and DG levels in DBA/2J mice, and to a lesser extent in C57BL/6J mice.
claims.source: Strikingly, in mice fed a western diet for 28 days to promote hepatic lipid accrual, PSMD9-antisense oligonucleotide treatment was associated with a significant attenuation of hepatic and plasma TG and DG levels in DBA/2J mice, and to a lesser extent in C57BL/6J mice.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on experimental validation performed in the Parker et al. study as described in the text.

claims.claim: The phenotypic outcome resulting from modulation of a gene is highly dependent on genetic background.
claims.source: Indeed, the phenotypic outcome resulting from modulation of a gene is highly dependent on genetic background, as others have previously demonstrated (Sittig et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study demonstrating the importance of genetic background in phenotypic outcomes.

claims.claim: The strain-specific effect of PSMD9 modulation is representative of the variable influence that modulation of a single gene would have on a complex trait in a human population.
claims.source: This strain-specific effect is representative of the variable influence that modulation of a single gene would have on a complex trait in a human population and underscores the importance of performing experimental validation in multiple strains with differing genetic backgrounds, where possible.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation of strain-specific effects in the PSMD9 validation experiments.

claims.claim: Cardiometabolic diseases are greatly influenced by biological sex.
claims.source: Cardiometabolic diseases are greatly influenced by biological sex.
claims.evidence: This reflects established knowledge about sex differences in cardiometabolic diseases.

claims.claim: It is important to incorporate both sexes in validation experiments, where possible, in line with efforts to promote inclusion of females in preclinical research.
claims.source: This highlights the importance of incorporating both sexes in validation experiments, where possible, in line with efforts to promote inclusion of females in preclinical research (Clayton and Collins, 2014; Heidari et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to policy statements promoting sex inclusion in research.

claims.claim: Sex hormones regulate key sex- and tissue-specific pathways in NAFLD.
claims.source: For example, this approach revealed that sex hormones regulate key sex- and tissue-specific pathways in NAFLD (Kurt et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study demonstrating the role of sex hormones in NAFLD.

claims.claim: Inclusion of sex as a biological variable in validation studies improves the applicability of findings and can facilitate personalized management strategies.
claims.source: Inclusion of sex as a biological variable in validation studies improves the applicability of findings and can, to an extent, facilitate personalised management strategies.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the importance of sex differences in disease and the benefits of including both sexes in research.

claims.claim: Hepatic expression of many of the 25 novel cholesterol-regulating genes identified by Li and colleagues was modulated in response to diets that modulate hepatic cholesterol levels.
claims.source: Using a variety of functional experiments to filter the genes, they demonstrated that hepatic expression of many of these genes was modulated in response to diets that modulate hepatic cholesterol levels, or in response to cholesterol depletion in mouse liver cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on experimental validation performed in the Li et al. study as described in the text.

claims.claim: Silencing of 10 of the 25 novel cholesterol-regulating genes altered the expression of Hmgcs in mouse liver cells.
claims.source: Furthermore, silencing of 10 of the 25 genes altered the expression of the regulator of cholesterol synthesis, hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA synthase (Hmgcs), in mouse liver cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on experimental validation performed in the Li et al. study as described in the text.

claims.claim: Sesn1 was functionally characterized to play a role in cholesterol biosynthesis using in vivo and in vitro systems.
claims.source: This led to the identification of several high-confidence, cross-species conserved, cholesterol regulating genes, such as sestrin1 (Sesn1), which was functionally characterised to play a role in cholesterol biosynthesis using in vivo and in vitro systems.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on experimental validation performed in the Li et al. study as described in the text.

claims.claim: Systematic, data-driven validation studies can be used to assign priority to candidate genes and provide insight into the molecular mechanism of a gene under investigation.
claims.source: This is an elegant example of how systematic, data-driven validation studies can be used to assign priority to candidate genes and provide insight into the molecular mechanism of a gene under investigation.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the example of the Li et al. study demonstrating this approach.

claims.claim: More extensive integration of data from human and mouse populations can be leveraged to maximise biological discovery and clinical translation.
claims.source: We have highlighted here the many potential advantages of comparing, overlaying, and integrating complementary datasets between mice and humans to improve these outcomes. Indeed, more extensive integration of data from human and mouse populations can be leveraged to maximise biological discovery and clinical translation.
claims.evidence: This is a concluding statement that summarizes the potential of cross-species integration as discussed throughout the manuscript.

claims.claim: Future studies must address the lack of consistency in phenotyping complex traits across species.
claims.source: In order to comprehensively and accurately integrate datasets from human and mouse populations, a number of key areas must be addressed. Firstly, future studies must address the lack of consistency in phenotyping complex traits across species.
claims.evidence: This is a recommendation for future research based on current limitations in the field.

claims.claim: Cross-species genetic maps need to be streamlined and require improved annotation of functional orthologues.
claims.source: Secondly, cross-species genetic maps need to be streamlined and require improved annotation of functional orthologues, so that more direct comparisons can be made between model systems and human biology.
claims.evidence: This is a recommendation for future research based on current limitations in the field.

claims.claim: Validation experiments should be viewed as an accompaniment, rather than a replacement for laboratory-based experimental validation.
claims.source: Lastly, while genomic tools and complementary human and mouse populations serve as useful sources of biological validation and mechanistic insight, these should be viewed as an accompaniment, rather than a replacement for laboratory-based experimental validation.
claims.evidence: This is a recommendation emphasizing the continued importance of experimental validation.

claims.claim: Performing validation experiments in both sexes and across multiple genetic backgrounds improves the biological relevance and translation of findings.
claims.source: Indeed, we emphasise the importance of performing validation experiments in both sexes and across multiple genetic backgrounds, where possible, to improve the biological relevance and translation of findings.
claims.evidence: This is a recommendation for best practices in validation studies based on the considerations discussed in the manuscript.

results.result: Cardiometabolic diseases represent a significant disease burden in developed countries and are influenced by both traditional risk factors and genetic factors, though individuals can present with disease in the absence of traditional risk factors.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 provide well-established background on cardiometabolic diseases, supported by appropriate citations (C4) and reflecting established clinical knowledge (C1-C3). These definitional and epidemiological claims are appropriately supported by the literature.

results.result: Genetics explains a substantial proportion of cardiometabolic disease risk (40-60% for CAD, 20-70% for NAFLD, 26% for HF), and these diseases are polygenic in nature with many loci identified through GWAS.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C9 are supported by appropriate citations to heritability studies and GWAS literature. The polygenic nature (C9) is appropriately inferred from the identification of multiple loci (C8). These claims accurately represent the current understanding of genetic contributions to cardiometabolic diseases.

results.result: Genetic mechanisms driving cardiometabolic diseases are largely conserved across mammalian species, making model organisms valuable complementary tools for exploring disease mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C11, C74, and C75 are well-supported by multiple citations demonstrating cross-species conservation. The inference that this conservation makes mouse models valuable (C11, C75) is logical and appropriately drawn from the cited evidence.

results.result: Mouse genetic reference panels overcome key limitations of human GWAS by enabling tight environmental control, access to tissues, and reproducibility across generations.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C13 and C31-C36 describe well-established advantages of mouse models. These are appropriately characterized as knowledge-based claims reflecting standard understanding in the field. The inference that these features overcome GWAS limitations (C34) is logical.

results.result: Systems genetics is an integrative methodology that explores relationships between genetics and phenotypes, building on the foundation of the Human Genome Project and GWAS approaches.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C18 provide appropriate definitional and historical context, with C15 supported by citation to the Human Genome Project. These foundational claims are well-established and appropriately presented.

results.result: Human GWAS have identified many disease-associated loci but face limitations including modest effect sizes, replication challenges, and the polygenic nature of complex diseases, with many loci residing in non-coding regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C25 accurately describe both achievements and limitations of GWAS, supported by appropriate citations (C19, C21, C23-C25) and established knowledge (C20, C22). These claims provide important context for the rationale of the review.

results.result: Polygenic scores aggregate the influence of multiple variants to predict disease risk and can complement traditional risk factors for clinical risk stratification and therapeutic target identification.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C28 are appropriately supported by citations to PGS literature. The claims accurately represent the utility and potential of polygenic scores in clinical and research contexts.

results.result: Integration of lipidomic analysis from the Busselton Health Study identified CAD susceptibility loci that co-localized with lipid loci, suggesting shared genetic etiology.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C30 are supported by citations to the Busselton Health Study. The inference of shared genetic etiology (C30) is appropriately drawn from the co-localization observation. This provides a concrete example of multi-omics integration.

results.result: Different mouse breeding strategies (inbred vs. outbred) offer distinct advantages, with comparable genetic diversity to human populations, stable genetics across generations, and the ability to apply various interventions and meta-analyses.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C43 describe properties of mouse genetic reference panels with appropriate citations (C38, C39, C40, C41, C42, C43). The comparison of genetic diversity between mice and humans (C39) is particularly well-supported with specific quantitative data.

results.result: The BXD panel consists of 198 strains with sufficient statistical power for mapping using 60-80 strains, has accumulated extensive phenotypic and omics data over 50 years, but captures lower genetic diversity than multi-parent populations.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C48 are well-supported by citations describing the BXD panel. The claims accurately present both advantages (C45-C47) and limitations (C48) of this resource, providing balanced assessment.

results.result: The Collaborative Cross and Diversity Outbred panels offer high genetic diversity and mapping resolution but face challenges including limited strain numbers (CC) and requirements for larger sample sizes and individual genotyping (DO).
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C54 accurately describe the CC and DO panels with appropriate citations. The discussion of trade-offs between genetic diversity and practical constraints (C53) reflects established understanding in the field.

results.result: The Het3 population, used primarily by the Interventions Testing Program, has identified several anti-aging compounds with favorable effects on metabolic and cardiometabolic traits, often in a sex-dependent manner.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C58 are supported by appropriate citations describing the Het3 breeding scheme and ITP studies. The findings regarding anti-aging compounds (C58) are well-documented in the cited literature.

results.result: The HMDP consists of 100+ diverse inbred strains with sufficient power to map complex traits and detect small effect sizes, with statistical methods available to account for population structure.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C64 are well-supported by citations to HMDP studies. The claims accurately describe the composition, statistical properties, and applications of the HMDP, providing appropriate context for the review's focus.

results.result: The Ath-HMDP, created by crossing transgenic atherosclerosis-prone mice with HMDP strains and feeding a western diet, identified novel genes associated with atherosclerosis and has been used to identify conserved pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C68 are supported by appropriate citations describing the Ath-HMDP design and findings. This represents a key application of the HMDP for studying atherosclerosis with human disease relevance.

results.result: The HF-HMDP, using isoproterenol treatment to model heart failure, has provided insights into genetic regulation of cardiac dysfunction traits and identified GPNMB as a potential biomarker.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 are supported by citations to HF-HMDP studies. The identification of multiple cardiac traits and a potential biomarker demonstrates the utility of this intervention-based approach.

results.result: The HF/HS-HMDP, using high-fat/high-sucrose diet intervention, has elucidated genetic mechanisms regulating hepatic lipids, NAFLD, and metabolic traits in a sex- and tissue-specific manner.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C72 are supported by multiple citations to HF/HS-HMDP studies. This intervention has been particularly productive for understanding diet-induced metabolic dysfunction.

results.result: The Ex-HMDP, using voluntary wheel-running exercise, identified novel mechanisms regulating mitochondrial biogenesis and bioenergetics in skeletal muscle.
results.evaluation: Claim C73 is supported by citation to the Moore et al. study. This represents an important application of the HMDP to understand beneficial metabolic interventions.

results.result: Research has shifted from variant discovery to functional elucidation in the post-GWAS era, with the discovery rate exceeding validation capacity, making cross-species integration valuable for prioritizing targets.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C78 accurately describe the current state of the field, with C77 supported by citation. The inference that cross-species integration helps address this challenge (C78) is logical and represents a key thesis of the review.

results.result: Despite structural differences (19 vs. 22 chromosome pairs), human and mouse genomes share ~30,000 protein-coding genes with ~80% showing 1:1 orthology and >99% having at least one orthologue, organized in conserved synteny blocks.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C83 are well-supported by citations to genome comparison studies. The quantitative data on orthology (C82) and the inference about duplication events (C83) are appropriately presented.

results.result: Human ApoE exists as three structurally and functionally distinct isoforms while mice have only one, illustrating species-specific differences in gene function.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C85 are supported by appropriate citations and provide an important example of functional differences between species that must be considered in cross-species studies.

results.result: The relative contribution of genes to disease varies with disease severity, and accurate quantification of complex disease progression is challenging, particularly for NAFLD/NASH where reliable biomarkers are lacking.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C89 reflect established understanding about disease complexity (C86-C87) with C88 supported by citation to the multiple-hit hypothesis. The discussion of biomarker limitations (C89) appropriately identifies a key challenge for cross-species integration.

results.result: Genetically supported therapeutic targets have more than double the success rate in clinical development, yet preclinical studies often use single strains that don't reflect population heterogeneity, with strain-specific responses to dietary interventions well-documented.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C94 are supported by appropriate citations. C90 provides important justification for genetic approaches, while C92-C94 document strain-specific responses that support the use of diverse panels.

results.result: Cross-species interrogation identified PVRL2 as a candidate gene for atherosclerosis through correlation with lesion size in the Ath-HMDP and co-localization with APOE/APOC1 near the human CAD-associated SNP rs2075650.
results.evaluation: While C96-C97 are supported by data, C98 is explicitly speculative. The correlation data (C97) does not establish causality, and the speculation about mediation (C98) requires experimental validation. This example illustrates potential but not proven cross-species utility.

results.result: Integration of human CAD tissue expression data with Ath-HMDP identified 30 CAD-causal modules, 46% of which associated with mouse atherosclerosis, including an aortic network regulated by seven key driver genes that were validated to modulate foam cell formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C105 describe the Talukdar et al. study with appropriate citations. The experimental validation (C105) strengthens the findings. This represents a strong example of successful cross-species integration with functional validation.

results.result: A glucose and lipid determining (GLD) module was identified and replicated across multiple human and mouse cohorts, with four key driver genes that are known cholesterol biosynthesis regulators, indicating evolutionary conservation.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C110 are supported by citations to the Cohain et al. study. The replication across multiple independent cohorts (C108) and the inference of evolutionary conservation (C110) are appropriately supported.

results.result: Adipose mitochondrial OXPHOS genes were elevated in female mice in the HF/HS-HMDP in a sexually dimorphic manner, conserved in human cohorts, with Ndufv2 identified and validated as a causal regulator of sex-specific obesity through mitochondrial function.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C115 describe the Chella Krishnan et al. study with appropriate citations. The cross-species conservation (C112), genetic mapping (C114), and experimental validation (C115) provide strong support for this sex-specific mechanism.

results.result: In DO mice, genetic variants in pancreatic islets associated with diabetes traits were identified, with syntenic regions significantly enriched for human diabetes-related SNPs.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C117 are supported by citations to the Keller et al. studies. The synteny-based enrichment analysis (C117) provides evidence for cross-species conservation of diabetes-related genetic architecture.

results.result: PSMD9 was identified and validated in the HMDP as a regulator of hepatic and plasma lipids, with hepatic PSMD9 expression associated with adiposity in UK Biobank and linked to obesity and T2D in GWAS.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C120 are supported by appropriate citations. The mouse discovery (C118), human validation (C119), and GWAS support (C120) demonstrate successful mouse-to-human translation.

results.result: GPNMB was upregulated in cardiac tissue but decreased in plasma in both mouse models and human heart failure, suggesting potential utility as a biomarker.
results.evaluation: While C121-C123 are supported by data from the Lin et al. study, C124 is explicitly speculative. The reciprocal changes in tissue vs. plasma are interesting but biomarker utility requires prospective validation studies not yet performed.

results.result: Integration of mouse liver co-expression modules with human lipid GWAS prioritized 48 genes (25 novel) below genome-wide significance, with many replicated in MVP and UK Biobank datasets.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C128 describe the Li et al. study with appropriate citations. The replication in independent human cohorts (C128) strengthens confidence in the prioritized genes.

results.result: Comprehensive comparison of 827 mouse atherosclerosis genes with 244 human GWAS-derived CAD genes revealed substantial pathway concordance (>50%), with expression of many orthologous genes correlating with lesion size and plasma lipids in the Ath-HMDP.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C135 describe the von Scheidt et al. study with appropriate citations. The comprehensive literature review (C129-C130) and quantitative assessments of concordance (C132-C134) provide strong evidence for cross-species conservation.

results.result: MAFF/Maff and ATF3/Atf3 were predicted to orchestrate liver networks linked to atherosclerosis and validated to regulate lipid metabolism in an inflammation-dependent manner.
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C137 are supported by citations to follow-up studies. The in silico prediction (C136) combined with in vitro validation (C137) demonstrates the value of network-based approaches.

results.result: Integration of Ath-HMDP liver data with human NASH data identified cis-eQTLs for Phactr2 and Eif3h correlating with fibrosis, with 60% overlap in NASH sub-networks and nine shared pathways between species.
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C141 describe the Hui et al. study with appropriate citations. The quantitative assessment of pathway overlap (C140-C141) provides evidence for both conserved and species-specific mechanisms.

results.result: Statistical causal inference and network modeling approaches are useful for prioritizing candidate genes but are prone to false positives due to correlated phenotypes and modeling limitations, requiring experimental validation.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C145 reflect established understanding about the strengths and limitations of computational approaches in systems genetics. The emphasis on validation (C145) is appropriate and important.

results.result: PSMD9 overexpression increased hepatic lipids while antisense oligonucleotide treatment reduced them, with strain-specific effects (stronger in DBA/2J than C57BL/6J) demonstrating the importance of genetic background.
results.evaluation: Claims C146-C149 describe validation experiments from the Parker et al. study. The strain-specific effects (C147-C149) provide important evidence for the value of testing interventions across multiple genetic backgrounds.

results.result: Cardiometabolic diseases are influenced by biological sex, with sex hormones regulating tissue-specific pathways in NAFLD, highlighting the importance of including both sexes in validation studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C150-C153 are supported by established knowledge (C150) and citations (C151-C152). The recommendation for sex inclusion (C151, C153) is appropriately supported by policy statements and scientific evidence.

results.result: Systematic validation of 25 novel cholesterol-regulating genes showed that many were modulated by cholesterol-altering diets, 10 affected Hmgcs expression, and Sesn1 was functionally characterized for its role in cholesterol biosynthesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C154-C157 describe the Li et al. validation approach with appropriate citations. This represents an exemplary systematic approach to prioritizing and validating candidate genes (C157).

results.result: More extensive integration of human and mouse data can maximize biological discovery and clinical translation, but requires addressing phenotyping consistency, improving ortholog annotation, and performing validation in both sexes across multiple genetic backgrounds.
results.evaluation: Claims C158-C162 provide appropriate concluding recommendations. C158 summarizes the review's thesis, while C159-C162 identify important future directions based on limitations discussed throughout the manuscript.
